subject: physics
title: Conduction and convection
key_idea: Conduction passes thermal energy through a material by vibrating particles. (Supplement) In metals, free electrons carry it too. Convection passes it through liquids and gases: warmed fluid becomes less dense, rises, and cooler fluid sinks to take its place.

blocks.text: Conduction is the transfer of thermal energy through a material without the material itself moving. This section explains how it happens in solids.

items.meaning: A material that transfers thermal energy well, such as a metal.
A material that transfers thermal energy badly, such as wood or plastic.
Electrons in a metal that are not fixed to one atom and can move through the whole metal.

items: (Supplement) The particles in every solid are held in a **lattice** and vibrate about fixed positions.
(Supplement) The hot end vibrates more strongly, so its particles pass energy to their neighbours by collisions.
(Supplement) The energy passes from particle to particle along the solid.
This is the only method in most non-metals, which is why they are generally poor conductors.
(Supplement) A metal also has **free electrons**.
(Supplement) The free electrons near the hot end gain energy and move through the metal.
(Supplement) They collide with atoms or ions further along and transfer energy to them.
This is much faster than lattice vibrations alone, so metals are **good conductors**.

blocks.text: (Supplement) Some solids conduct better than thermal insulators but less well than good conductors. Glass is an example.

items: Conduction needs no movement of the material itself.
All solids conduct by lattice vibrations.
Metals also conduct using free electrons, so they conduct best.

blocks.text: Gases and most liquids are poor conductors. This section explains why, in terms of particles.

items: (Supplement) The particles in a gas are far apart, so collisions are rare.
(Supplement) The particles in a liquid are closer but can move around, so energy is passed on less well than in a solid.
Gases and most liquids have no free electrons to carry energy.
Trapped air is a very good insulator, which is why wool, fur and foam keep things warm.
Fix identical rods of different materials so that one end of each is heated equally.
Attach a drawing pin to each rod with wax, at the same distance from the heat.
The pin on the best conductor falls first.
Alternatively, put strips of different materials in hot water and time how long the heat takes to reach the top.
Gases are poor conductors because their particles are far apart.
Liquids are also poor conductors, because energy passes on slowly.
Compare materials by timing how fast heat travels along identical rods.

blocks.text: Convection transfers thermal energy through liquids and gases by the movement of the fluid itself. It cannot happen in solids.

items.text: The fluid is heated and its particles gain energy.
The fluid expands, so the particles move further apart.
The warm fluid is now less dense than the fluid around it.
Cooler, denser fluid sinks and takes its place, and the process repeats.

blocks.text: This circulating flow is a **convection current**. At the top the fluid cools, becomes denser again and sinks.

diagram.alt: A loop showing a convection current: fluid is heated, expands and becomes less dense, rises, cools and becomes more dense, then sinks and is heated again.
steps: It expands and becomes less dense

items: Drop a crystal of potassium permanganate in a beaker of water and heat the water just below the crystal. The coloured water rises and circles round.
Put a candle under one chimney of a box with two chimneys, and hold smoke over the other. The smoke goes down the cool chimney, across the box and up the chimney above the candle.
Convection happens only in liquids and gases.
Warm fluid is less dense, so it rises.
Cool, denser fluid sinks and replaces it, forming a convection current.

blocks.text: Most real situations involve more than one method. Radiation, the third method, is covered elsewhere.

items: A kitchen pan has a metal base so the heat conducts quickly to the food, and a plastic or wooden handle so it does not burn your hand.
A radiator warms a room by convection. Air next to it is warmed, rises, and cooler air flows in at the bottom.
(Supplement) A fire burning wood or coal heats the room mainly by radiation. Convection carries hot gases up the chimney, and conduction passes energy through the coal and the metal grate.
(Supplement) A car radiator conducts heat from the hot engine coolant through its metal walls to the air. Convection moves the warm air away, and some energy is radiated.

Heat passing through the base of a pan
Heat passing from a hot drink through the wall of a metal mug
Warm air rising from a radiator
Hot water rising to the top of a kettle

items: Metal is used where heat must pass quickly, and plastic, wood or trapped air where it must not.
Rooms are heated by convection currents.
Real situations often combine conduction, convection and radiation.

checks.q: (Supplement) Explain why a metal conducts thermal energy better than wood.
checks.a: A metal has free (delocalised) electrons that move through it and carry energy, as well as lattice vibrations. Wood has only lattice vibrations.
The warm air expands, so it is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it rises.

checks.q: Why can convection not happen in a solid?
checks.a: The particles in a solid cannot move from place to place, so there can be no flow of hot material.

checks.q: (Supplement) Explain why a gas is a poor thermal conductor.
checks.a: Its particles are far apart, so they collide rarely and pass on little energy.

worked_example.question: Two containers are each filled with hot water. The outer surface of the metal container is hot. Explain how electrons transfer thermal energy through the metal of the container.
answer_points: The delocalised electrons gain energy from the lattice vibrations of the atoms nearest to the hot water.
The electrons move through the metal.
Collisions between the electrons and remote ions or atoms transfer thermal energy to all parts of the metal container.
worked_example.tip: Any three score one mark each. Say that the electrons move and that they collide.

worked_example.question: The air near the bar of a large hurdle on an athletics track receives energy by heating. Explain how a convection current is formed in the air near the bar.
answer_points: The temperature of the air increases.
The air expands, so its particles move further apart.
The density of the air decreases.
Cool air replaces the warmed air.
worked_example.tip: Any four score one mark each. Link the change in density to the air rising.
